A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DREsS dataset and CASE augmentation work. Text, equations, figures, tables, and all appendices are readable and support matching content across the substantial expansion and reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original AES results, a CASE augmentation ablation, and comparisons of language models and prompting strategies in Section 4 and Appendices B–C.

after.justification: v2 retains original AES experiments and adds reannotation results, Llama and GPT-4o evaluations, and quantitative and qualitative analyses of synthetic essays.

M1.justification: Sections 3.2–3.3 retain the same rubric-standardization weights, corruption equation, and content, organization, and language corruption operations. Added language models are evaluation comparators; no change to the proposed CASE procedure is established.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation of synthetic essays themselves, including GPT-4o-generated inputs, for target-score fidelity and learner-language realism in Sections 5.2–5.3. The original 22 prompts, student population, and standardized dataset sources remain; their increased sample counts alone do not expand coverage.

E2.justification: v2 replaces gpt-3.5-turbo with gpt-4o in the scoring comparisons, adds supervised Llama 3.1 8B in Tables 3–4, and introduces GPT-4o generation as a comparator to CASE in Table 5. EASE, NPCR, BERT, Longformer, BigBird, and GPT-NeoX remain.

E3.justification: Reported DREsSNew and CASE sizes change from 1,782 and 20,601 to 2,279 and 40,185. Few-shot scoring changes from two examples to five. New protocols include reannotation of 227 essays by five experts and generation comparisons sampling 900 essays per method across nine score levels. These changes do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds annotation-agreement validation, score-distribution analysis, CASE-versus-GPT-4o score-fidelity testing, linguistic-feature comparisons, and an illustrated essay case study. The original augmentation-volume ablation remains, moving from Figure 1 to Figure 3.

E5.justification: v2 adds ± dispersion summaries for generated scores and linguistic features, plus significance markers for ANOVA/Tukey comparisons in Table 6. The ± quantity is not explicitly defined. The original instructor-distribution tests and seed 22 remain, with no added repeated-run uncertainty reporting for AES scores.

E6.justification: Existing BERT, EASE, NPCR, and earlier fine-tuned-model scores remain unchanged. v2 adds Llama total QWK scores of 0.466/0.563/0.691 and GPT-4o five-shot QWK of 0.428; GPT-3.5 results are replaced under different conditions. New findings include annotation κ = 0.193 and mean synthetic-score agreement of 0.661 for CASE versus 0.225 for GPT-4o.

T1.justification: The corruption equation and its assumptions are unchanged. Neither version contains theoretical propositions or proofs, and v2's added empirical metrics do not introduce new mathematical definitions or derivations.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion enlarge the claimed dataset contribution from approximately 1.7K to 2.3K classroom essays and 20K to 40.1K synthetic essays. The central DREsS/CASE contributions, reliability claim, and reported 45.44% baseline improvement remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking score imbalance to instructor grading behavior and argues that CASE better preserves learner errors and offers greater control than LLM generation. It contextualizes weak reannotation agreement as substantial and removes v1's cross-dataset non-robustness argument about EASE/NPCR. The dedicated limitations section remains substantively unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly identifies DREsSNew as the validation/test source, adds annotator provenance and generation prompts, revises hardware specifications, and documents separate hardware for large models. It also supplies a dataset access link and a datasheet covering licensing and maintenance. The original training hyperparameters remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of Kumar et al. (2022), distinguishing trait-assisted holistic scoring from DREsS's rubric-based objective. Additional references support Llama, grading behavior, readability metrics, and datasheet documentation. The broader positioning around scarce, inconsistent, expert-annotated AES data remains intact.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is substantially reorganized: language-model and prompting comparisons move from appendices into Section 4, the ablation moves into a dedicated Discussion & Analysis section, and appendices are reorganized around settings, prompts, and a datasheet. Much of the original introduction and method prose is retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds a dataset overview graphic, score-distribution plots, synthetic-quality tables, and color-annotated essay examples. Earlier appendix result tables are consolidated into main-text Table 4; rubric and prompt tables are reformatted and widened. The original ablation plot is retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: v2 improves empirical scrutiny and transparency through reannotation, direct synthetic-fidelity checks, broader comparators, and clearer evaluation and access documentation. These gains are limited by overinterpreting κ = 0.193, a purported same-prompt case study displaying different essay topics, and unrelated CSRT/red-teaming wording in the new datasheet. The additions help readers assess the work but do not resolve its central reliability concerns.
